title: Pasura (Sn 4.8)
hookLine: read it: debaters who want to win
tomorrow: a father offers the Buddha his daughter's hand. what's the answer?

lines: WARM FACE, SET JAW, FAST THUMBS.
cards: Midnight, a comment thread, and someone is wrong. Feel what happens. The face goes warm.
The jaw sets. The thumbs move fast. There's a little jolt when the perfect reply lands, and a sour drop when theirs is better.
An old poem knows that body exactly. Its debater is Pasura, and he's walking around like a champion fed on royal food, roaring for someone to take him on. And the Buddha tells him: nobody's here.

teach.b: In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata. Only here is purity, the debaters say, and nowhere else. Hungry for argument, they plunge into the crowd and call each other fools.
In the middle of the assembly, anxious, wanting praise, one of them loses, and he's crushed. He grieves and complains: he beat me. Another wins, and he laughs and swells up with it.

Then the line that turns it: that swelling is the very ground of his distress. Winning and losing feed the same hunger, for praise. So, the poem says, don't argue to win; the skilled say purity doesn't come that way.
Then the Buddha speaks to Pasura directly. Like a champion raised on the king's food, you go roaring for a rival. Go find one somewhere else.
Here there's nothing left to fight.

teach.h: THE WINNER SWELLS. THE LOSER GRIEVES.
teach.b: Listen to the sounds in the poem: the roar, the laughing winner, the complaining loser.
And then the quiet of the one who simply won't step into the ring.
No need to win isn't losing on purpose.

how: Debate is a formal part of training in some Buddhist monasteries, especially in Tibetan traditions, where it sharpens understanding; teachers draw on poems like this one to warn against arguing for praise or to win.

o: a king who judged debates between teachers
a monk who won every argument he entered
a debater told there's no one here to fight

games.q: the debater's poem — tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, winning the debate brings lasting satisfaction
the winner swells with pride, and the poem calls that swelling the ground of his distress.
the Buddha tells Pasura there's nothing here to fight
go roaring somewhere else, champion; here there's no rival.
the poem says never to speak about the teaching at all
it warns against arguing to win and for praise, not against speaking.

games.q: in class, someone states a fact wrong and you could correct them in front of everyone. by the poem, what's worth checking first?
o: whether you want the fact fixed, or want the win.
nothing; correct them loudly, because truth comes first.
nothing; stay silent, since speaking up is only ego.
games.why: the poem doesn't ban speaking. it looks at the hunger underneath: winning and losing both feed the wish for praise. the fact can be fixed without the roar.

practice: Bring to mind one argument you're itching to win. Notice where it lives in the body: warm face, tight jaw, a fist.
Then, one breath at a time, let the out-breath unclench one place, the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, and listen to the room go quiet around a fight you decided not to feed.

wordCard.voice: Pasura: the roaring debater of the eighth poem, told that whether you win or lose, the fight feeds the same hunger, and there's no one here to fight.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the wandering debater the poem addresses; the poem is the Pasūra Sutta.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: no need to win, since the ring is optional. Eight poems, halfway through the chapter.

drop.name: the chapter of eights, read whole
